records.place: Pirque, with the Don Melchor vineyard at Puente Alto, Maipo Valley, Chile

wine.name: Don Melchor Cabernet Sauvignon
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, the great majority, with small parts of Cabernet Franc, Merlot and Petit Verdot, each from parcels of its own.
wine.sites: The Don Melchor vineyard at Puente Alto, on stony alluvial ground on the north bank of the Maipo at about 650 metres, at the foot of the Andes: seven parcels of Cabernet Sauvignon, Parcel 1 among them, planted in 1979, beside smaller parcels of the other three grapes.
wine.making: Each parcel, and each smaller lot within it, is picked and fermented on its own, and the blend is chosen each year from well over a hundred lots with a consultant from the Médoc. Some fifteen months in French oak barrels follow, about seven in ten of them new, before bottling.
wine.glass: Blackcurrant and blackberry with red cherry, violet and rose, a note of pencil lead and the fresh mint of the Alto Maipo; fine grained, firm tannin and a long, fresh finish. Age brings cedar, coffee and dark chocolate.
wine.ageing: Tight for its first eight to ten years in a strong vintage, it then keeps and develops for a quarter of a century and more.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or two, an old one gently off its sediment; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The founder's name, Melchor Concha y Toro, given to the wine with its first vintage, 1987.
The denomination of origin: the Alto Maipo area on the north bank of the river, at the foot of the Andes.
The grape named on the label, the great majority of the blend, with small parts of three others.

records.table: First made in 1987 and named for the house's founder, Don Melchor is Concha y Toro's Cabernet from stony ground at Puente Alto, at the foot of the Andes. Blackcurrant, violet and Andean mint ride on fine, firm tannin; decant it young.
records.story: Melchor Concha y Toro (1833 to 1892), a Santiago lawyer, deputy and minister of finance, founded the house in 1883 at Pirque, on land owned by his wife, of the Subercaseaux family. As the company tells it, he planted varieties brought from Bordeaux, and a French oenologist came to oversee the first harvest. In 1921 the family made the house a company, its shares held among themselves, and those shares were first traded on the Santiago exchange in 1933. Its fine wine began across the river, at Puente Alto. In 1984, as Viña Don Melchor's own timeline records, Émile Peynaud (1912 to 2004) tasted Cabernet from its Puente Alto vineyard, saw the promise of the ground and proposed his collaborator in the Médoc to lead the work. The first vintage, 1987, was named Don Melchor for the founder. From 1997 the vineyard was studied parcel by parcel, and each parcel has since been picked and fermented apart. In 2019 Don Melchor left the Concha y Toro range to stand as a winery of its own, Viña Don Melchor, within the group. Of the three Puente Alto Cabernets on a Chilean list, Don Melchor is the eldest, begun nine years before Almaviva and twelve before Viñedo Chadwick.

report: The land through the founder's wife, the Bordeaux varieties, the French oenologist at the first harvest, family hands until 1921 and the listing of 1933 rest on the company's own 20-F filing of 2019 on vinacyt.com, read in a search summary, which did not fit among the five sources.

Peynaud's dates are those the Codex's other flagship records cite from Wine Spectator's obituary; his collaborator in the Médoc and that collaborator's son, who blends Don Melchor with the house, are described rather than named.

Melchor Concha y Toro died on 21 June 1892 in the parliamentary library and 21 July in Wikipedia, so the record gives the year alone; his ministry of finance (1869 to 1870) is in Wikipedia and its mirrors.
The library calls Don Melchor Chile's first icon Cabernet; the record avoids the claim, and the house's filings call it the first ultra premium wine of the Chilean industry.

One account dates the first planting at Puente Alto to 1890 and another has Concha y Toro buying the Tocornal estate there in 1968; neither found a second source, so both are left out, as is the vineyard's size (125 or 127 hectares).
The ageing line rests on the long verticals reported by Club Oenologique (1988 to 2022) and a twenty five year tasting reported in Dallas; it is a judgement, not a measured fact.

wine.name: Almaviva
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, by far the larger part, with Carménère next and, in most vintages, small parts of Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot or Merlot.
wine.sites: Puente Alto vineyards set aside for Almaviva in the Alto Maipo, on poor, stony alluvial soils that drain freely, cooled each night by cold air from the Andes.
wine.making: The grapes are cooled and left on their skins, then warmed for fermentation in stainless steel tanks sized to each parcel, with a final maceration; the malolactic follows on its own. The wine spends about ten months in the Grand Chai, then moves to a second year cellar, for sixteen to twenty months in all in French oak barrels, most of them new.
wine.glass: Cassis and black cherry over graphite and cedar, with a lift of roasted red pepper and paprika from the Carménère and a touch of dark chocolate; full and polished, with fine grained tannin and fresh acidity.
wine.ageing: Approachable young for its build, it opens fully after about ten years, and a strong year keeps well beyond twenty.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius in a Bordeaux glass; give a young bottle an hour or more in a decanter, and take an old one gently off its sediment.

label.means: Count Almaviva, hero of The Marriage of Figaro, his name printed in the playwright's own handwriting.
Three reproductions of a stylised Mapuche design, a vision of the earth and the cosmos, for Chile.
The origin on the label: an Alto Maipo area at the foot of the Andes, shared with Don Melchor.

records.table: Concha y Toro and the Mouton Rothschild company first made Almaviva in 1996 from Puente Alto: Cabernet Sauvignon led, with Carménère adding a lift of roasted red pepper. Its label pairs a count from The Marriage of Figaro with a Mapuche design.
records.story: The wine came before the company. Its first vintage, 1996, was made from Concha y Toro's Puente Alto vineyards under the joint direction of the Chilean house and the Bordeaux company that Baron Philippe de Rothschild (1902 to 1988) had built around Château Mouton Rothschild, which had already made Opus One in Napa with the Mondavi family. In 1997 his daughter, Baroness Philippine de Rothschild (1933 to 2014), who had succeeded him at Mouton in 1988, and the chairman of Concha y Toro signed the agreement that created Almaviva, one Franco Chilean wine from one estate. Its international launch came in 1998, and the estate built a winery designed by a Chilean architect, its curved roof meant to echo the Andes. The name and the label tell of the two cultures: Count Almaviva is the hero of The Marriage of Figaro by Beaumarchais (1732 to 1799), and the label prints the name in the playwright's own handwriting beside three reproductions of a stylised Mapuche design, a vision of the earth and the cosmos. A second wine, Epu, the Mapuche word for two, followed in later years. For a sommelier, Almaviva completes the set of French ventures abroad with Opus One in Napa and Cheval des Andes in Mendoza, and it is the one of the three that carries Carménère.

wine.name: Casa Real Cabernet Sauvignon
wine.grapes: Only Cabernet Sauvignon, from old massal selections of the grape on their own roots.
wine.sites: Old, ungrafted Cabernet at Alto Jahuel on the Andean side of the Maipo, on alluvial soils over a clay subsoil: the Carneros Viejo block, which gave the first vintage, and in later accounts a second old sector nearby.
wine.making: The first vintage, 1989, was fermented in large wooden casks, and later vintages in stainless steel. Ageing is in French oak barriques, for about fourteen months in the vintages of the 2000s and for eighteen to twenty months, most of the barrels new, from 2018 onwards.
wine.glass: Red plum and cassis with cedar, tobacco leaf and a faint roasted green pepper; medium bodied for Maipo Cabernet, its dusty, fine tannin lifted by fresh acidity. Old bottles turn to leather, prune and cigar box.
wine.ageing: Reserved for its first decade in a strong vintage; the house gives it twenty years and more, and the 1989 showed well when tasted at twenty four years old.
wine.serve: A Bordeaux glass at 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; an hour in a decanter for a young bottle, and a gentle decanting off the sediment for an old one.

label.means: The name of the wine, the house's old vine Cabernet Sauvignon from Alto Jahuel, first made with the 1989 vintage.

records.table: Since 1989 Santa Rita has bottled Casa Real, its Cabernet Sauvignon from old, ungrafted vines at Alto Jahuel, first from the Carneros Viejo block. Cedar, tobacco leaf and red plum over dusty tannin make it the old school face of Maipo Cabernet, and it ages for decades.
records.story: The house tells a story older than its vineyard. In 1814, by its account, 120 soldiers of the independence army took refuge at Alto Jahuel in the house of Paula Jaraquemada (1768 to 1851), which stands on the estate; Chile's council of national monuments tells it of 1818, after the patriot defeat at Cancha Rayada. Viña Santa Rita itself was founded on the estate in 1880 by a Santiago businessman, and from the late nineteenth century until the middle of the 1970s it belonged to the family of his son in law, the García Huidobros. In 1972 the estate's park, houses, chapel and cellars were declared a historic monument, and in 1980 the Claro group bought into the house. Its familiar 120 range is named for the soldiers of the legend. Casa Real came with the 1989 vintage, when Cabernet from one old block, Carneros Viejo, was first bottled on its own. Decanter later named the 1989 one of its Wine Legends. Casa Real is the classic Cabernet of a nineteenth century Maipo house, a counterweight to the view that Chilean quality began in the 1990s.

others.note: The familiar range, its number taken from the soldiers who, in the estate's story, sheltered at Alto Jahuel.

others.name: Medalla Real

wine.name: Lota
wine.grapes: A larger part of Cabernet Sauvignon with Merlot, the share moving with the vintage.
wine.sites: The old blocks of the Macul estate at the foot of the Andes, which Santiago has grown around: Cabernet Sauvignon planted in 1932 and Merlot from about 1980. The importer's sheet for 2020 also names the family's Buin vineyard.
wine.making: Fermented in stainless steel tanks, with the malolactic fermentation to follow; the wine is then aged about fifteen months in French oak barriques, most of them new, before bottling.
wine.glass: Blackberry, cassis and black cherry with cedar, tobacco leaf and a touch of dark chocolate, the Merlot rounding the middle; full bodied, with ripe, firm tannin and a long, savoury finish.
wine.ageing: It stays firm for five to eight years, then keeps and gains for fifteen years and more in a strong year.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or two; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The wine's name, shared with the coal port near Concepción whose mines the founder worked.

records.table: For its hundred and fiftieth year, in 2006, Cousiño Macul launched Lota, a blend of old vine Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot from the Macul estate that Santiago has spread around. Expect blackberry, cedar and a touch of dark chocolate, with ripe, firm tannin and a long, savoury finish.
records.story: The Hacienda Macul, at the foot of the Andes on the edge of Santiago, was bought in 1856 by Matías Cousiño (1810 to 1863), whose fortune grew with the coal mines he worked at Lota, on the coast near Concepción; the house counts that year as its founding. His son and his son's wife renewed its vines in the 1860s, bringing, as the house records, Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot from Pauillac, Chardonnay from Burgundy and Sauvignon from Martillac. A Cabernet harvest of 1927, in the house's telling, gave rise to Antiguas Reservas, the line it calls its emblem. By the 1990s Santiago had spread around the estate, and in 1996 the family bought land at Buin, further south in the Maipo, while the historic cellars and the old vines stayed at Macul. Lota was launched in 2006 to mark the house's hundred and fiftieth year: a blend of Cabernet Sauvignon from vines planted in 1932 and Merlot from about 1980, both from the old estate. It shares its name with the coal port where the founder worked the mines. Against the Puente Alto blends, Lota is the old Santiago house's answer, grown on a vineyard the city has surrounded.

report: Not in the library: each date rests on the house's own pages and a second source (Winebow's brand page and sheets, the parliamentary library of Chile, Memoria Chilena) or is hedged as the house's; 1856 is the year Matías Cousiño bought the Hacienda Macul, from which the house dates itself.

The region record's producers line names Antiguas Reservas as the house's long lived Cabernet; the plan's Lota is the wine the house presents as its flagship, launched in 2006, and the record keeps Antiguas Reservas among the others.
That Lota is named for the coal town was found only on a personal blog, not on the house's or the importer's pages, so the record says only that the wine shares its name with the town.

The son and daughter in law who renewed the vines are described: Luis Cousiño's dates (1835 to 1873) are in Wikipedia and Memoria Chilena, but Isidora Goyenechea's death is 1897 in one and 1898 in the other; the house dates the French cuttings to 1860 on one page and the Bordeaux journey to 1863 on another, so the record says the 1860s.
Matías Cousiño's birth is 1810 in the parliamentary library and Wikipedia, 1802 in one Memoria Chilena account; the record keeps 1810.
The Merlot's planting is 1980 or 1981 in different accounts, so the record says about 1980; one 2019 note gives 1960 for the Cabernet, against 1932 in the house's own pages and Winebow's.
Barrel time is about fifteen months, some 85 per cent new French oak, in Winebow's sheets for 2018 and 2020; Winebow's brand page says eighteen months, and the record keeps the sheets.
The Buin purchase of 1996 rests on Winebow's brand page and a Wine-Searcher note; Lota's first vintage (2003 or 2004 in different accounts) is left out.

wine.name: Viñedo Chadwick
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, alone in many vintages, with a few per cent of Petit Verdot in some since 2016.
wine.sites: The family's old polo field at Puente Alto, a single vineyard of stony alluvial ground on the Maipo's north bank, at about 650 metres where the Andes begin; planted from 1992.
wine.making: Lot by lot, the fruit ferments in small tanks, of stainless steel and in some vintages concrete, and stays on its skins for eighteen to forty days by lot and year. The malolactic follows in oak, and the wine is aged about twenty two months, most of it in new French oak barrels and a share in large oak foudres.
wine.glass: Blueberry, cassis and dark cherry with liquorice, fresh mint and a touch of bitter chocolate; silky and tightly knit rather than broad, its fine, gravelly tannin set against fresh acidity.
wine.ageing: Firm in youth, it opens after about a decade when the vintage is strong and keeps for twenty years and more.
wine.serve: Pour at 16 to 18 degrees Celsius into a Bordeaux glass, a young bottle after an hour or two in a decanter.

label.means: Spanish for the Chadwick vineyard: the wine takes the family's name and comes from one vineyard.
The wider origin this label gives; the vineyard itself lies at Puente Alto, on the valley's Andean side.

records.table: Viñedo Chadwick's 2000, from the family's old polo field at Puente Alto, planted in 1992, placed first at the Berlin Tasting of 2004, ahead of Château Lafite. It is the Cabernet of the family behind Viña Errázuriz, its blueberry and liquorice carried on silky, fine tannin.
records.story: The Errázuriz house was founded in 1870 in the Aconcagua valley, north of Santiago, but its Maipo wine began as a sports ground. The family's patriarch, a polo player, had built his home and a polo field on an estate he bought at Puente Alto, the old Viña San José de Tocornal; by the family's account, the land reform of the 1960s led him to sell most of it, but he kept the house and the field. In 1992, at his son's suggestion, the field was planted with Cabernet Sauvignon; he did not live to taste its first vintage, and the wine is named in his memory. The first vintage was 1999. On 23 January 2004, in Berlin, the family set Chilean wines blind beside Bordeaux first growths and Italian reds before thirty six European critics and writers: sixteen wines of 2000 and 2001 in all. Viñedo Chadwick 2000, only its second vintage, placed first and Seña 2001 second, with Château Lafite 2000 third. Petit Verdot joined the blend in small measure with the 2016 vintage, while the warm 2020 went back to Cabernet alone. The Berlin result is the date to know: Chile's own blind tasting coup, held in Berlin and not in Paris, and won by a Puente Alto Cabernet from a former polo field.

traps: The Berlin Tasting was held in Berlin in January 2004, not in Paris and not in the 1970s; Viñedo Chadwick 2000 placed first.
Viñedo Chadwick is Puente Alto, in the Maipo; Seña, from the same family, is Aconcagua.
Don Melchor and Almaviva share the Puente Alto subzone but are Concha y Toro's wine and its venture's, not the Chadwick family's.

sources.title: Decanter: Surprise result for Margaux and Lafite against New World

report: The library's founded year, 1999, is the first vintage; the vines were planted on the polo field in 1992 (The Drinks Business, Decanter, Vinous), and the field itself is older.

The patriarch is described rather than named: his death in 1993, the year after the planting, is in The Drinks Business and Club Oenologique, but his birth year was not found in two sources (one account gives 1929 to 1996); the estate's purchase (1942 or 1945), his captaincy of Chile's polo team and the polo club he helped found are left out.

Lafite 2000 in third place is in Decanter's report and two other accounts (Académie du Vin, a Canadian magazine); the lower placings differ between lists and are left out, as is the later run of the tasting in other cities.

The making rests on the importers' sheets (Hatch Mansfield for 2013 to 2015, Mark Anthony for 2020): about twenty two months, 73 to 80 per cent new French oak, with Stockinger foudres from 2013; the Petit Verdot and the all Cabernet 2020 are on the estate's own past vintages page.

changed: wine.grapes, story and cards[1]: Petit Verdot planted in 2011 meets vines planted in 2005 in one listing of the 2021, so the planting year is cut; its arrival with the 2016 stands (97 and 3 per cent by one listing).

wine.making: concrete in later vintages, after eighteen to thirty days on skins; the 2013 sheet names concrete and the 2014 and 2015 sheets steel alone, with eighteen to thirty days in 2013 and twenty three to forty in 2015, so now concrete in some vintages and eighteen to forty days, the malolactic in oak as the sheets say.

story and cards[0]: he died the following year: The Drinks Business, Decanter's profile and Club Oenologique give 1993, but one account gives 1929 to 1996; now he did not live to taste its first vintage, true on either year.

story: the old Viña San José de Tocornal stands, now on the estate's own Legacy page (bought in 1942; Decanter says 1945, so no year is given), which also tells of the sale of most of it after the land reform of the 1960s, the house and the polo field kept; that is added as the family's account, and it fits Forbes Chile's purchase of a Tocornal estate at Puente Alto by Concha y Toro in 1968.
story: the event most often cited for Chile's modern standing in fine wine is a rank with no measure behind it, and is cut.
story: the hot 2020 is now warm, Decanter's word for an early ripening year.

table and traps[2]: the Errázuriz family's Cabernet; the family is the Chadwicks, Errázuriz by descent and the owners of Viña Errázuriz, so now the family behind Viña Errázuriz and the Chadwick family's.
